skill.name: Kinds of backing: evidence, expert, example
skill.why: Different backing does a different job. Knowing the kind helps you judge it.
skill.how: Numbers or records? Evidence. Someone who knows? Expert. One real case? Example.

beats.say: Backing holds up a claim. It comes in three kinds.
Evidence is numbers or records you could check.
beats.show: **Rangers counted half as many bilbies as ten years ago.**

beats.say: An expert is someone who knows a lot about it.
beats.show: **Dr Lin, a bilby scientist,** says they need help.

beats.say: An example is one real case that shows it.
beats.show: **Last week, a bilby called Pip lost her burrow in a fire.**

beats.say: So ask: numbers, a person who knows, or one case?

weDo.text: Claim: Our school needs shade sails over the playground. Backing: Dr Patel, a skin doctor, says children need shade when they play outside.
weDo.prompt: What kind of backing is this?
weDo.hint: Who is talking? Do they know a lot about skin?
weDo.success: Dr Patel is a skin doctor, so she knows a lot about sun and skin. That's an expert.

options.reason: There are no numbers or records here. It's what one person says.
Nothing happened to one person here. Think about Dr Patel's job.

weDo.prompt: Gus claims Mo's cooking is dangerous. Match each piece of backing to its kind.

weDo.success: A count of smoke alarms is evidence. A chef is an expert. The melted spoon is one real case.

encounters.text: Last week, the Bugle asked readers whether the council should give more money to the Bluster Rock Primary school band. One said the band brought 500 people to its last concert. Another sent us a long letter from a music teacher. A third told us how the band changed one shy student's life. Some readers wrote in to say the money should go to the footy club instead. The council will vote on the money next month.

encounters.text: Dear Editor, I coach the Bluster Rock Roos, our town's junior footy team, and I am writing to ask the council to put lights on the oval at Red Dune Park. In winter, the sun sets before 5:30 pm, and by the time our players get to training, there is barely an hour of daylight left. encounters.frame: Year 6 is debating sugary drinks at the canteen. The Kindalah is sorting their backing.
encounters.text: On Thursday, Year 6 held a debate in the library about whether the Bluster Rock Primary canteen should stop selling sugary drinks. The team arguing for a ban came prepared. They had numbers from the canteen, quotes from people who know about health and teeth, and stories from real students. The healthy-food team wore green T-shirts and had practised their speeches all week. Their captain, Priya, opened by holding up a can of soft drink and asking the audience to guess how many teaspoons of sugar were inside. Most people guessed three. The answer was nine, and several Year 5s gasped. Mo was the timekeeper, although he kept stopping the clock to ask whether jelly counts as a drink. The other team argued that students should be free to choose, but they ran out of time after their mascot, a giant cardboard can, fell on the judges. Here are six pieces of backing the ban team used. Principal Okafor has promised to read the best arguments at assembly.

encounters.text: Dear Councillors, I am writing on behalf of the Bluster Bay Turtle Volunteers to ask you to cancel the licence that allows jet ski hire in the bay. For decades, the northern end of the bay has been a nesting beach for green turtles, and every summer, our volunteers count the nests, fence them off and watch the hatchlings scramble down to the water. Each nest holds around a hundred eggs, and the hatchlings come out at night, guided by the moonlight on the water. Since the hire shop opened in October, our work has changed. The hire shop has twelve jet skis, and on a busy Saturday, all twelve are out on the water at once, often within metres of the shore. I know that the hire shop brings visitors to our town, and I do not want anyone to lose their job. I have gathered backing of every kind for my claim that jet skis are hurting the turtles: the rangers' figures, the views of people who study turtles for a living, and the stories of individual animals we have tried to save. I have listed four sentences below, but my nephew has warned me that one of them isn't really backing at all. I would be grateful if you could read them before the vote on 12 December. Yours faithfully, Ada Pennick, turtle volunteer

encounters.frame: The Bugle has printed an opinion piece about the music festival. The Kindalah is sorting it, feather by feather.
encounters.text: BRING BACK THE FESTIVAL: an opinion piece by Jojo Reyes of Red Dust Static. The Bluster Rock Music Festival has not been held since 2019, and I believe the council should bring it back next autumn. Some people say a festival is too noisy, too expensive and too much trouble for a small town. I understand those worries, and I don't want to pretend they aren't real. Like many people my age, I first heard live music at that festival, sitting on my dad's shoulders in the dust and watching a bush band play until midnight. Our band still has a faded festival T-shirt from that year, and our drummer wears it to every gig for luck. But I have spent the last month gathering backing for my claim that a festival would be good for Bluster Rock, and I think the case is strong. I spoke to shopkeepers, read the council's own reports, interviewed people who study tourism and music, and listened to locals who remember the old festivals. Below are six pieces of the backing I found. I hope that readers will judge each one on its merits. If the council agrees, three local bands have already offered to play for free, and the old flatbed truck behind the footy club could serve as a stage.
encounters.prompt: Match each piece of backing to its kind.
encounters.success: Takings, reports and surveys are evidence. Professors and planners are experts. Single stories, however moving, are examples.

items.reason: A professor who researches tourism knows the topic well. She's an expert.

encounters.success: One koala's broken promise is a single real case. That makes it an example, however telling.

parts: WHERE DID THE MONEY GO? Last month, Maxx Vantablack auctioned his painting 'Gold on Gold' for $40,000 and promised that every cent would go to the Maxx Vantablack Rescue Fund. The Bugle has been trying to find out what the fund actually spends its money on, and so far, the answers have raised more questions than they have settled.

parts.tap: The fund's own published accounts show that only $3,000 of the $90,000 it raised last year was spent on animal care.
parts.reason: Published accounts with figures are evidence you could check.

parts.tap: Ms Harriet Cole, an accountant who checks the books of charities, says that a fund spending so little on its main purpose should be investigated.
parts.reason: An accountant who checks charities knows how they should spend money. She's an expert.

parts.tap: Last year, the fund promised to pay for an injured koala's operation at the Red Dust Wildlife Rescue, but the money never arrived, and volunteers paid for it themselves.
A spokesperson for Maxx said the fund was 'doing amazing things' and that 'the haters just don't understand'.
parts.reason: This isn't backing for the report's claim. It's Maxx's side, and it gives no proof.

parts: The Bugle has asked to see the fund's receipts for the past three years. We will report what we find. Readers who have donated to the fund are encouraged to ask for receipts too.

encounters.frame: Gus's robotics club proposal has a labelling problem. The Kindalah found it straight away.
encounters.text: Gus has finally been given five minutes at the school council meeting to argue for a robotics club at Bluster Rock Primary. He has prepared three pieces of backing, one of each kind, and Indi has helped him label them on a poster so that the council can see exactly how strong his case is. First, he has a quote from Professor Dana Liu, who designs robots for hospitals and believes that every primary school should teach children to build simple machines. Second, he has the results of a national study, which found that schools with robotics clubs had a 20 per cent rise in the number of students choosing science subjects in high school. Third, he has the story of Saltbush Creek Primary's robotics club, whose team of Year 6 students built a robot that waters the school garden and won a state prize. Unfortunately, Indi was drawing a robot in the margin while she labelled, and one label went on the wrong piece of backing. Gus has rehearsed his speech eleven times, mostly in front of Mo, who now says the words along with him. He is also bringing his own robot, Sorty, which sorts recycling with two claws made from salad tongs, to show the council what students can build.
encounters.prompt: Tap the wrong label on Gus's poster. Then choose the right one.
encounters.success: A study measuring a 20 per cent rise across many schools gives figures you could check. That's evidence.

parts: Professor Dana Liu's view:

parts.tap: expert
parts.reason: That's right. A professor who designs robots knows the topic well.

parts: . The national study's results:

parts.tap: example

parts: . The Saltbush Creek story:

parts.tap: example
parts.reason: That's right. One school's club is a single real case.

options.reason: A study isn't one person who knows a lot. It reports measured results from many schools.
A 20 per cent rise is a measured result, not what someone thinks.
The study does back up Gus's claim. It gives results you could check.

encounters.frame: Four companies have sent backing to the Vantamart buyers. The Kindalah is sorting their pitches, nose held.
encounters.text: Every month, the Vantamart's buyers listen to pitches from companies that want their products on its shelves, and this month's theme is 'Gross but Good'. This time, the buyers have asked each company to send one piece of backing for its main claim, and they have been very clear about what they want. They are tired of companies that simply shout that their product is the best. Instead, they want to know what kind of backing each company is offering, so that they can decide how much to trust it. Some buyers prefer numbers from careful tests, some prefer the word of people who really know the field, and some are most moved by a single real story. Last month's winner, a burping water bottle, sold out in three days and was advertised on Maxx's stream for a whole month. This month, the winning product will be stocked in every Vantamart on the island and sold in a special gold box. The four companies have each sent in a single sentence, and the buyers have printed them below. Maxx will make the final decision himself, after he has tried every product live on his stream. Gus has asked for free samples of all four, and Mo has asked whether any of them are edible.
encounters.prompt: Which company's backing is an example?
encounters.success: One family's dog going without a bath is a single real case. That makes it an example.

options.text: Our seashell toothpaste removed 30 per cent more plaque than ordinary toothpaste in a test of 200 people.
options.reason: A test of 200 people with a percentage is evidence you could check.

options.text: Dr Felix Ward, a germ scientist at the national university, says our sock spray kills the bacteria that cause foot odour.
options.reason: Dr Ward knows a lot about germs. He's an expert, not an example.

options.text: The Patel family's dog, Rufus, wore our stink-proof collar for a whole month and never once needed a bath.
Our glow-in-the-dark slime is simply the greatest, slimiest and most glorious slime that has ever existed.
options.reason: This is just a claim shouted loudly. It doesn't give any kind of backing.

encounters.frame: The Bugle has a follow-up story on the mystery lights. The Kindalah is reading it under the doona.
encounters.prompt: The report claims the lights are probably not ghosts. Tap the expert.
encounters.success: Dr Okafor studies glowing fungi, so she knows exactly what natural glows look like. She's an expert.

parts: MYSTERY LIGHTS: NOT GHOSTS AFTER ALL? For two weeks now, strange green lights have been appearing above the old mine at the back of Bluster Rock, and ghost tour guide Slick Vinnie has been telling visitors that they are the spirits of long-gone miners. Ticket sales for his midnight tour have tripled. But the Bugle has found growing reasons to think that the lights have a far more ordinary explanation.

parts.tap: Readings taken by the council over five nights show that the lights appear only when the air is warm and damp.
parts.reason: Readings over five nights are measured records. That's evidence.

parts.tap: Dr Esther Okafor, a scientist who has studied glowing fungi for thirty years, says the colour matches a fungus that grows on old mine timbers.
Last Thursday, a local teenager, Kade, crept into the mine's entrance with a camera and photographed a glowing patch on a wooden beam.
parts.reason: Kade's photo is one real case, from one night. That makes it an example.

parts.tap: Most sensible people already know that ghosts don't exist, so the answer was obvious from the start.
parts.reason: This isn't backing. It just tells you the answer is obvious without showing why.

parts: Slick Vinnie has not commented, although a box of green glow sticks was seen in the back of his ute on Tuesday. The Soggy Biscuit crew has offered to help the council investigate, and their engineer, Gus, has asked for permission to take a small sample of the fungus home for testing. Mo has asked whether it can be eaten.
